threads.thread_goal: Align on current changeover steps and pick the pilot line scope.

messages.text: Morning all. To get T1 moving for the Standardise Assembly Line Changeover and Ergonomic Routines project, can we write down how we actually do a changeover today on each line? Things like: when we stop, who starts clearing parts, when we adjust tools, quick safety checks, and when we restart. Please include any shortcuts you see people using, even if they are not ideal. We will use this to fill A8 and then tidy it up. Also, we need to agree which line and shift we use as the pilot, so share which one you think is most stable and has a mix of experienced and newer people.

On my line, for the small motor housings, we usually do it like this: 1) Supervisor calls changeover about 10 minutes before end of batch. 2) We let the last pieces run through, then stop the belt. 3) One person clears finished parts and leftover components into the right bins. 4) Another person starts swapping jigs and small tools. 5) We do a quick wipe down of the station and floor if there are any spills. 6) Then we load the new parts and do a test run of 2 or 3 pieces. We do not always stop to adjust the working height or reach, even though we should. Timing wise, it is around 20 to 25 minutes if nothing jams.

On the larger motor parts line, the pattern is similar but a bit slower: 1) We get a heads up about 15 minutes before. 2) We let the last units clear and then lock out the station if we need to go inside the guarded area. 3) Two of us remove heavy fixtures and store them on the rack. 4) We bring in the new fixtures and check they are pinned correctly. 5) We adjust torque settings and check the tools are in the right place. 6) One person does a quick visual check for loose bolts or oil on the floor. 7) We run 5 trial pieces and the supervisor signs off. This can take 30 to 40 minutes, especially if we have to wait for maintenance. I also see people skipping the floor check when we are in a rush, which is not great for slips.

On night shift on the small parts line, we often do it a bit differently because there are fewer of us. We still get the call, but sometimes it is only 5 minutes before. We stop the line, then one person tries to do almost everything: clear parts, swap tools, and clean. The other person is usually finishing paperwork. We rarely do a full test run; we just check the first piece and then go. It can be 25 to 35 minutes, but it feels messy. I am not sure how much detail you want here. Do you need exact minutes for each step or just rough order like this?

This is helpful. For T1, I think we need enough detail so we can see where time goes and where we cut corners. Maybe not second by second, but at least: who does the step, what they do, and a rough time range. For example: clear finished parts, 1 person, about 5 minutes. That way we can spot bottlenecks and unsafe shortcuts for A8. Does that level sound ok to everyone, or do you think we should go deeper?

That level works for me. If we also note any checks we skip when we are tired or rushing, it will help us design something that fits real life. From my side, I can map the large motor line on day shift with that structure: step, who, time, and any risk I see. We can then compare with the small parts line and see which one is more stable for the pilot.

I can add more detail for the small parts line on early shift using that format. I will try to time a changeover today if we get one, even if it is just with my watch. I will also note when we skip adjusting the working height or moving heavy boxes closer, because that is when backs start to hurt.

From the time records side, I see that the small parts line on day shift has fewer long stoppages and more consistent changeover durations. The large motor line has more variation and more calls to maintenance. If we want a clean pilot for the Standardise Assembly Line Changeover and Ergonomic Routines project, I would suggest we pick the small parts line, day shift, as the first test. It will also make it easier later when we link this to the weekly summary template and time coding.

If we start with small parts line day shift, can we still include some notes from night shift in A8? Our pattern is different because of fewer people, and I do not want us to design something that only works when the line is fully staffed.

Yes, we should definitely capture night shift patterns in A8, even if the formal pilot is on day shift. That way, when we update the SOP later, we can check that the steps still work with fewer people. For the pilot scope, I agree with using the small parts line, day shift, as the main test, and we will tag any night shift differences in the feedback log.

To make sure we are aligned on detail for T1, I will write each step like this: 1) Stop line and clear last units, 2 people, about 5 to 7 minutes, risk: people step over parts on the floor. 2) Remove fixtures, 2 people, 10 minutes, risk: lifting heavy items without help. 3) Clean and check floor, 1 person, 3 minutes, risk: sometimes skipped. If we all follow a similar pattern, it will be easier to compare lines and see where we can standardise.
Got it, I will follow that pattern. I will focus on the small parts line day shift steps so we have a clear base for the pilot, and then we can add notes from other shifts into A8 as we go.

threads.thread_goal: Draft and refine the new changeover SOP and visual guides.

messages.text: I have put together a first draft of the changeover steps for the small parts line day shift based on what we mapped in T1. It is in A1 as Pilot Line Changeover SOP v1. The structure is: 1) Prepare for changeover (call, heads up, gather tools), 2) Stop and clear line, 3) Swap fixtures and tools, 4) Clean and ergonomic checks, 5) Trial run and sign off. Can you read through and comment on anything missing or unclear? We also need to think about which key steps should go onto the wall posters in A4, so they are easy to see during the rush.

I went through A1. The flow makes sense, but I think we should be more explicit about safety and ergonomics in a few places. For example, in the stop and clear step, we should add: confirm line is stopped and any guards are in place before reaching in. In the swap fixtures step, we should say: use two people for any fixture above a certain weight, and adjust working height before lifting. These details will slow us down a little on paper, but they match what we want to see on the floor and will help reduce minor incidents.

I like that the steps are numbered and short. One thing I noticed: in the clean and ergonomic checks section, it says to adjust working height and move heavy boxes closer, but it does not say who is responsible. On our shift, that usually falls between people and sometimes no one does it. Maybe we should assign it clearly to the person doing the cleaning step, so it does not get missed.

I have a question on the trial run part in A1. It says run 3 pieces and get supervisor sign off. On night shift, we do not always have a supervisor right there. Should we write an option like: if no supervisor is present, second worker checks the first 3 pieces and notes it in the log, and the supervisor reviews at the next visit? I do not want us to block the line waiting.

Good points. I will update A1 to: 1) Add a clear lock and check line stopped step before anyone reaches in. 2) Specify two people for heavy fixtures and adjusting height before lifting. 3) Assign ergonomic checks to the person doing cleaning, as suggested. For the trial run, I like the idea of a second worker check when the supervisor is not there. We can write it as the standard option for nights and weekends.

From my side, the main thing is that the SOP in A1 is clear enough that we can later measure changeover time consistently for the weekly summary in A6. The current draft defines start as when the supervisor calls changeover and end as when the first good piece is approved. That is workable, but we should make sure everyone understands it the same way. Maybe we can add a short note in the SOP and on the poster that says: changeover time is from call to first good piece.

Agree. If we do not define start and end clearly, the numbers in A6 will not mean much. I suggest we keep it simple: start at the moment the line stops for changeover, end when the first good piece is confirmed. The call can happen a bit earlier and is not always consistent. That way, the people on the floor can see it easily.

I like using line stop to first good piece as the timing. It is easier for us to see on the floor. For the posters in A4, I think we should only show the main flow: 1) Stop and make safe, 2) Clear and swap, 3) Clean and adjust, 4) Trial pieces and confirm. The detailed notes like two people for heavy lifts can stay in A1, but we can use icons on the poster to remind people.

For A4, can we also add a simple reminder about checking the floor for spills and trip hazards before restarting? Maybe a small icon near the clean and adjust step. That is one of the things we skip when we are tired, and a visual nudge would help.

So for A4 we are saying: posters show the 4 main steps plus a few key icons: lock and make safe, two people for heavy lifts, adjust height, check floor, and trial pieces. The full wording, roles, and timing stay in A1. I will adjust the draft of T5 to match this split.

With those updates, I am comfortable using A1 as the first pilot version for the small parts line day shift. It covers the main steps, assigns responsibilities, and includes the key safety and ergonomic checks. We can still tweak after the first weeks, but it is good enough to start training and testing.

Agreed. The steps in A1 are clear for me, and the split with A4 will help on the floor. Once we have the posters printed, we can do a quick walk through on the line to see if anything still feels confusing.

threads.thread_goal: Define ergonomic checklist and rotation schedule for the pilot.

messages.text: I have drafted some initial items for the ergonomic workstation checklist in A2 for the small parts line pilot, linked to T3. The idea is that it can be done in under 5 minutes at the start of the shift or after a changeover. Current items: 1) Working height set between hip and elbow level. 2) Parts and tools within easy reach, no twisting. 3) Heavy boxes placed at waist height, not on the floor. 4) Clear floor, no spills or loose parts. 5) Enough space to move without bumping into others. Please add or adjust items so they fit what you see on the line.

These look good. I would add one more: 6) Check that you can keep your wrists straight when using tools, not bent up or down. On my station, if the tool is too high or too low, my wrists start to ache by mid shift. It is a quick check but makes a big difference.

Could we also include a reminder to swap hands or change posture if possible? Maybe something like: 7) Plan at least one small posture change or micro break each hour. I know we cannot always stop, but even a few seconds to stretch or change stance helps, especially on nights.

These are all good suggestions. We just need to keep A2 short enough to do in under 5 minutes. Maybe we can group them: posture (height, wrists), reach (tools and parts), lifting (box height, two person lifts), and environment (floor clear, space to move). That way the checklist is 4 or 5 lines, but we can explain the details during training.

Agreed. I will reword A2 into 5 grouped checks: 1) Posture: height and straight wrists. 2) Reach: tools and parts close, no twisting. 3) Lifting: heavy items at waist height, use help when needed. 4) Floor: no spills or loose parts. 5) Space: enough room to move safely. That should still be doable in under 5 minutes at the start of the shift.
That grouping works for me. It is easy to remember and explain to others. Once the health and safety officer has a look, I think we can lock this list for the pilot and see how it feels in practice.

Switching to rotation for T4 and A3: for the small parts line, I suggest we rotate between three key stations every 2 hours within the same shift: 1) Feed and prep station, 2) Main assembly station, 3) Packing and final check. That way no one stays on the same repetitive task all day. The rotation would fit around the existing breaks: start on station 1, move to 2 after first break, then to 3 after lunch, and back if there is time. What do you think, especially for nights?

On nights we are usually only two on that line. Rotating between three stations might be tricky if we also have to cover breaks. Maybe for nights we define a simpler pattern in A3: swap between feed and main assembly every 2 hours, and share packing when needed. That way we still change tasks but do not leave a station uncovered.

For day shift with more people, the three station rotation sounds fine. We just need to make sure the timing lines up with our breaks so we are not swapping in the middle of a busy run. Maybe we can set the rotation points as: after first break and after lunch, as you said, and keep it that simple in A3.

To keep A3 clear, we can write two patterns: one for day shift with three stations and one for night shift with two stations. Both would still fit within the existing shift and break structure. We should also add a note that any worker with a medical restriction can stay on a suitable station, agreed with the supervisor.

Sounds good. So for the pilot we will: 1) Use the grouped ergonomic checklist in A2 with 5 items. 2) Use a rotation pattern in A3 with three stations for day shift and two for night shift, both tied to existing breaks. If everyone is ok with that, I will finalise T3 and T4 for the pilot run.

threads.thread_goal: Clarify time coding, payroll impact, and weekly reporting.

messages.text: I want to check how the new changeover and rotation routines will show up in time records for the Standardise Assembly Line Changeover and Ergonomic Routines project. For T7 and T12, we need clear rules in A7 so that changeover time and rotation activities are coded the same way on all shifts. Right now, some teams log changeover as general downtime and others do not log it separately at all. Can we agree what counts as changeover time and whether rotation checks are part of normal work or a separate code?

Based on A1, I would say changeover time should be from when the line stops for changeover until the first good piece is confirmed. That includes cleaning and ergonomic checks linked to the changeover. The regular ergonomic checklist at shift start could stay as part of normal work. For rotation, I see it as part of normal work too, not a separate code, unless the supervisor decides otherwise for a special case.

From the floor view, it would be simpler if we just have one code for planned changeover and keep everything else as normal production time. The more codes we have to remember, the more likely we are to make mistakes. For rotation, we are just moving between stations, so I would not separate it unless there is a long pause.

I agree with keeping it simple. One question: if a changeover runs long because of a problem, do we still code all of it as planned changeover, or do we split the extra time as unplanned downtime? That might matter for the weekly summary in A6.

Good point. For A7, I suggest we define: planned changeover time is the standard duration we expect for that line, and any extra time due to breakdowns or missing parts is coded as unplanned downtime. That way A6 can show both the average planned changeover and the extra time lost to issues.

As long as the rule is simple to explain, that works. Maybe in A7 we can give an example: if normal changeover is 25 minutes and it takes 40 because a tool breaks, we code 25 as planned changeover and 15 as unplanned downtime.

Yes, I can add that example into A7. On overtime and allowances for T7 and T12: the new routines should not change how overtime is calculated. Changeover and rotation time will still count as working time. The only change is that we will see planned changeover more clearly in the reports. I will double check sample payslips to be sure nothing odd happens.

So to summarise the coding rules for A7: 1) One code for planned changeover from line stop to first good piece, up to the standard duration. 2) Any extra time due to problems is unplanned downtime. 3) Rotation and regular ergonomic checks are part of normal work. If everyone is ok with that, we can treat this as our agreed rule set for the pilot.

That summary matches what we discussed and is easy to explain on the floor. For the weekly summary in A6, it would be useful if we can see average planned changeover time and number of incidents or near misses from A5 side by side, so we can spot if rushing is causing problems.

For T8, I have set up A6 to show: 1) Average planned changeover time per week. 2) Total extra time as unplanned downtime. 3) Count of incidents and near misses from A5. 4) A notes field for any special events. I will own filling this in for the pilot, using the time records and the incident log.
Looks good. Just to confirm, there are no changes to how our base pay or overtime is calculated, right? Only the way we label the time in the system.

Correct. For T12, I will confirm with a few sample payslips, but the plan in A7 is that pay rules stay the same. We are only making the time coding clearer. I will also prepare a short note for workers explaining what they might see on their time sheets, so there are no surprises.

threads.thread_goal: Run pilot check-in, review incidents and feedback, and decide updates.

messages.text: End of week check in for the small parts line pilot on the Standardise Assembly Line Changeover and Ergonomic Routines project. For T9 and T10, can you share: 1) How the new SOP in A1 and posters in A4 felt during changeovers, 2) Any incidents or near misses you logged in A5, and 3) Any suggestions for tweaks. I will capture everything in A8 so we can decide what to update in T11 and whether we are ready to extend beyond the pilot line.

On day shift we had three changeovers using A1 and the posters in A4. Overall it went smoother than before. The poster helped us remember the clean and adjust step, and we actually did the floor check every time. We had one near miss where a box was still on the floor in the walking path, but we caught it before anyone tripped and logged it in A5. My main suggestion: the wording about trial pieces could be shorter on the SOP, as people skim it.

On nights we used the SOP in A1 twice. The main difference was the trial run: we used the second worker check when the supervisor was not around, as written. That worked fine. We had one small incident where someone lifted a heavy fixture alone even though the poster shows two people. No injury, but we logged it in A5. Maybe we need a clearer icon or a stronger reminder in the briefing.

I joined one of the day shift changeovers to observe. Compared to our old way, the new flow in A1 reduced the wandering around looking for tools. The ergonomic checklist in A2 was done at the start of the shift and after one changeover; it took about 3 minutes each time. People said it was easy to remember because of the grouped items. I noted a few questions about what to do if the line is very busy and there is pressure to skip the clean and adjust step.

From the data side, A6 shows that average planned changeover time on the pilot line this week was 24 minutes, slightly better than before, and we had 2 short periods of extra time coded as unplanned downtime. A5 has 1 near miss and 1 minor incident as you mentioned. Nothing in the time coding suggests a pay issue, and the rules in A7 seem to be working as expected.

Thanks for the feedback. I will add to A8: 1) Shorten the trial piece wording in A1. 2) Make the two person lift icon more obvious on A4. 3) Emphasise in the briefing that the clean and adjust step is not optional, even when busy. Are there any steps in A1 that felt unnecessary or could be merged without making things less safe?

The only part that felt a bit long was the separate mention of checking tools and then checking fixtures. We could probably merge those into one step: check tools and fixtures are set and secure. That would make the list shorter without losing anything important.

I agree with merging those checks. Also, on nights we sometimes read the poster more than the full SOP. Maybe we can add a small line at the bottom of A4 saying: see SOP for full details, and make sure the SOP is easy to find near the line.

From what I saw, I would not remove any safety or ergonomic checks. The main improvements are about clarity: shorter sentences, merged checks, and stronger icons. We should also add a short note in A1 about what to do if there is pressure to skip steps: pause, call the supervisor, and record it in A5 if needed. That will help people feel supported when they follow the routine.

Based on this, I propose the following updates for T11: 1) In A1, merge tool and fixture checks, shorten trial piece wording, and add the note about not skipping steps under pressure. 2) In A4, make the two person lift icon bigger and add a small line pointing to the full SOP. 3) In A2, keep the grouped checklist as is, since it seems to work. If no one objects, I will treat these as the agreed changes to implement after the pilot.

From the numbers in A6 and the logs in A5, I do not see any reason to hold back the rollout. Changeover time is stable or slightly better, and incidents are low and well documented. As long as we apply the T11 updates, I think we can say the pilot line is ready and start planning to extend the routines to the other lines.

I agree. The workers I spoke with on the pilot line said they would keep using the new routine. There is some adjustment, but they see the benefit in fewer aches and less confusion. Once the T11 updates are in place, I think we can brief the other lines and start a phased rollout.
